description: We are Vilnius Tech robotics and mechatronics, ai engineering students, that love to solve hard challenges and look for opportunities to develop our skills.
summary:
We built a star research web app. You enter a star’s name or its sky coordinates, and the app plays SPHEREx images of that patch of sky like a short video, so you can see what moves or changes brightness over time.

The challenge asks for a public tool that makes SPHEREx data easy for anyone to explore. Our app hides the technical work and brings several astronomy sources into one place.

It matters because humanity’s future is in space, and star research will be a big part of it. Our app lets anyone take part, not only experts.
details:
What it does and how it works
The user picks a position in the sky. The app asks NASA’s SPHEREx archive (IRSA) which images cover that spot, downloads a small cutout of each one, lines them up on the same sky grid, and plays them in date order. It can also show difference frames, where one date is subtracted from another so that moving objects stand out. The coordinates are stored in the page link, so any view can be shared.

Benefits and intended impact
No downloads, coding or astronomy training are needed. We want students, hobbyists and volunteers to be able to look through SPHEREx data and spot moving or variable objects that nobody has noticed yet.

Tools and data

  • Python, Flask, Astropy and NumPy for fetching and processing the images
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the page
  • SPHEREx data from NASA/IPAC IRSA
  • Aladin Lite (CDS), SIMBAD, astrometry.net, the Gaia and DSS sky surveys, and the Anthropic API
  • Gaia and the ESA-hosted sky survey are space agency partner data (ESA)

How it is creative
It combines many separate astronomy services in one simple page and turns raw scientific files into something you can watch.

What we considered

  • The archive is slow, so the app saves what it downloads and keeps popular stars ready to open quickly.
  • SPHEREx images are low resolution and each detector sees different colours, so we only compare images from the same detector.
  • Nearby stars move quickly, so we used their current positions, not old catalogue ones.
dataRefs: NASA SPHEREx open data on AWS (nasa-irsa-spherex)
